evidence_cards.title: MEPS 2016: people with a reported ICD-10 A69 (other spirochetal infections, which includes Lyme disease)
evidence_cards.definition: People with at least one condition record whose 3-character ICD10CDX equals A69.
evidence_cards.method: Sum of unique-person weights (PERWT16F) over the domain; standard error by Taylor linearisation over VARSTR/VARPSU. Person-level, one year only.
comparability: A69 is the broad category that contains Lyme (A69.2x); MEPS public files keep only the first 3 characters, so this is NOT a Lyme-specific count and must not be read as Lyme prevalence.
MEPS panels overlap across adjacent years: never add or pool these yearly totals.
Condition rows come from household reports coded by professional coders.

AHRQ (MEPS team, 2026-09-24) urges caution forming Lyme cost estimates from MEPS: pooling 2016-2024 gives only about 300-400 observations, expenditures are highly skewed (about 1,000 or more are needed for a solid mean), only treated Lyme is identified (zero-expenditure cases drop out, biasing upward), events may be flagged as arthritis without naming Lyme, comorbidities cannot be separated from Lyme, and onset dates are not recorded. Lyme-specific A69.2 is available only in restricted data centers.

uncertainty.note: Small samples give very wide, unreliable intervals.

evidence_cards.summary: 2016: about 436,208 people (95% CI 250,739 to 621,678; 31 sampled persons) reported a condition coded A69.
evidence_cards.how_to_use: Cross-check or population context only, never a prevalence of Lyme or Long COVID; not a cost estimate (events are counts, not dollars).

provenance.collection_note: Respondent-reported conditions and hours, coded to ICD-10 by MEPS abstractors; not a clinical record.
provenance.computed_by: Computed in code from the federal file; no AI model
provenance.relevance: A69 is the broad category that contains Lyme (A69.2x); MEPS public files keep only the first 3 characters, so this is NOT a Lyme-specific count and must not be read as Lyme prevalence.
provenance.reliability: 31 sampled persons with a design-based standard error.

evidence_cards.title: CDC Lyme disease reported cases by year, 1992-2007 (national totals)
evidence_cards.unit: reported cases (national sum of aggregate cells)
evidence_cards.definition: Confirmed cases only under the era-specific national surveillance definition.
evidence_cards.method: Sum of the frequency column over all aggregate rows, by year and case status (matches the row counts of the no-geography line list).
comparability: A reported surveillance case is not the same denominator as a diagnosed-and-treated insurance episode; claims-based studies commonly estimate several times more.
Do not combine eras: the surveillance definition changed in 2022 (most cases are then classed "Probable"), so compare confirmed-plus-probable totals, not confirmed alone.
evidence_cards.summary: 1992-2007: annual reported cases (confirmed plus probable) range 8,257 to 27,444; confirmed alone 8,257 to 27,444.
evidence_cards.how_to_use: Cross-check the document's national case count or incidence for the same year, and state whether the two are on the same definition.

evidence_cards.definition: Edited annual hours adults report spending on their own visits and prescriptions, on others' visits, on medical bills and insurance, and on health care paperwork; plus the share who cared for a friend or family member in the past 30 days. Reported per week, month or year and converted to hours per year.
evidence_cards.method: Weighted mean (ESAQ person weight ESAQWT24F) with a Taylor-linearised standard error from VARSTR and VARPSU; adults who skipped an item are excluded from that item.
evidence_cards.source_locator: MEPS HC-256 (2024 Full-Year Consolidated): EQMVAM53, EQOVAM53, EQMBAM53, EQPPAM53, EQCARE53, ESAQWT24F
comparability: All U.S. adults who answered the questionnaire, not people with Lyme disease or Long COVID: MEPS cannot identify either condition reliably (AHRQ, 2026-09-24).
Fielded in 2024 only: the questionnaire was funded for that year, so there is no trend and no later update.

Self-reported. MEPS top-coded the annual hours at the 99.5th percentile (Table 13 of the HC-256 documentation: 2,080 hours for own visits, 1,040 for others' visits, 720 for bills, 520 for paperwork), so a few very large values are capped. About 6% of respondents skipped each time item, and MEPS notes that about 20% of those who completed the paper version gave no answer to them.
Hours, not dollars. Converting hours to dollars needs a published wage or value-of-time source shown next to the estimate.

scientific_analysis.disease_focus_rationale: The entire document is a biostatistical review of four NIH-funded randomized, placebo-controlled trials evaluating antibiotic retreatment for patients with persistent symptoms following standard treatment for Lyme disease (Lyme borreliosis); Long COVID is never mentioned.
scientific_analysis.plain_language_summary: This is a 2012 biostatistical re-analysis of the four NIH-funded randomized controlled trials (Klempner x2, Krupp/STOP-LD, Fallon) that underlie most guideline recommendations against antibiotic retreatment for patients with persistent symptoms after standard Lyme disease treatment. The authors argue the trials were often underpowered or used excessive design treatment effects, so their 'no significant benefit' conclusions do not prove retreatment is ineffective; they find that Krupp showed a statistically significant fatigue benefit and Fallon found a cognitive-function result at the margin of significance that was not sustained. The review also reports the adverse-event counts from these trials, including serious events such as sepsis and anaphylaxis. It does not report any dollar costs, productivity loss, insurance/access data, or Lyme disease case counts or prevalence figures - its focus is entirely on trial design, statistical power, and treatment-effect interpretation, not economic burden.

contextual_issues: The document states that 'long-term persistent illness following antibiotic treatment is not uncommon, particularly when treatment is delayed,' but gives no number for how common this is or how it varies with delay.

The document notes that trial populations showed 'significant morbidity...similar to that of multiple sclerosis or congestive heart failure' but does not quantify this comparison with a shared metric.
The document states future oral antibiotic regimens are 'likely to be safer...and less costly than ceftriaxone,' a qualitative cost comparison with no dollar figures attached.

SF-36 physical and mental component summary scores document reduced health-related quality of life in trial participants, but these are quality-of-life instrument scores, not economic burden measures.

The paper describes disagreement in the medical community over whether retreatment is beneficial and over guideline interpretation, implying repeated care-seeking and treatment-decision uncertainty for patients, but does not quantify care-seeking frequency or cost.
evidence_gaps: No direct medical cost data (e.g., cost of a course of IV ceftriaxone, cost of managing adverse events such as sepsis or anaphylaxis) are reported anywhere in the document.
No data on productivity loss, missed work, caregiving time, or other indirect costs associated with persistent Lyme disease symptoms.
No diagnostic-delay cost or care-utilization/navigation-burden data; the trials report only clinical outcome measures (SF-36, fatigue scales, cognitive tests), not health-service use or cost.
No long-term (beyond 6 months) outcome, relapse, or cost data; trial follow-up windows are limited to 12/24 weeks (Fallon) or 6 months (Klempner, Krupp).
No population-level prevalence, incidence, or case-count data for persistent Lyme disease symptoms that would be needed to scale any trial-level finding to a population burden estimate.
comparison_boundaries: The four RCTs (Klempner seropositive n=78, Klempner seronegative n=51, Krupp n=55, Fallon n=37) enrolled structurally different populations with different entrance criteria (broad symptom-based criteria for Klempner; severe fatigue [FSS-11≥4.0] for Krupp; objective memory impairment plus prior ceftriaxone treatment for Fallon) and measured outcomes over different time windows (3 and/or 6 months for Klempner/Krupp; 12 and 24 weeks for Fallon efficacy/durability). Their treatment-effect estimates and adverse-event counts must not be pooled or presented as a single low-to-high range, since the differences reflect distinct trial populations and follow-up windows, not merely varying confidence around one true effect.

No dollar cost figures, price years, or productivity/income-loss data appear anywhere in this document; any economic-burden claim about Lyme disease retreatment must be sourced elsewhere and must not be merged with this document's clinical-trial symptom-improvement or adverse-event figures.

The adverse-event counts (Krupp: 6/55; Fallon: 7/37 = 18.9%) are trial-arm-level RCT findings at 3-6 month follow-up, not annualized or lifetime population rates, and must not be extrapolated to annual incidence or lifetime risk without an explicitly labeled assumption.

subgroup_disaggregation_caveat.pooled_value: The Krupp et al. STOP-LD adverse-event count (6 significant AEs / 55 enrolled patients, 4 serious) and the Fallon et al. adverse-event rate (18.9%, 7/37 patients) are each reported as single pooled trial-arm figures with no breakdown by sex, age, race/ethnicity, disability status, or any other subgroup.

systemic_gap_caveat.description: The document describes an evidentiary/diagnostic-pathway gap: because no sensitive laboratory test for active B. burgdorferi infection is clinically available, treatment guidelines for persistent Lyme disease symptoms rely entirely on four RCTs that the authors argue were underpowered or analyzed with inefficient statistical methods, so clinical practice recommendations against retreatment rest on a contested evidence base rather than a validated diagnostic pathway.
systemic_gap_caveat.basis: Stated in the Introduction: 'Until a sensitive laboratory test for active infection is clinically available, clinical trials evaluating retreatment in persistently symptomatic Lyme disease patients provide the cornerstone of treatment guideline recommendations,' combined with the paper's critique that IDSA, AAN, and EFNS guidelines based recommendations on trials the authors found to be underpowered or improperly analyzed.

decision_relevance.summary: This document is a methodological critique of the RCT evidence base behind Lyme disease retreatment guidelines, not a cost-of-illness study, so a simulator built from it can only responsibly convey trial-level clinical outcomes and adverse-event risk, not dollar costs or productivity loss. Care delivery teams and guideline developers could use it to understand why the four foundational NIH-funded trials may have been under-powered or misinterpreted, informing how confidently 'no benefit' claims should be treated in clinical decision-making. Patients and advocates could use the adverse-event figures (e.g., 6/55 in Krupp, 18.9% in Fallon) alongside the reported efficacy findings to weigh retreatment risk-benefit discussions with clinicians. Payers/policy audiences would need to look elsewhere for actual cost, utilization, or productivity-loss data, since none appear in this document.
use_cases: A clinician or guideline-panel user could compare the trial-level adverse-event rates (Krupp: 6/55 AEs, 4 serious; Fallon: 18.9% AE rate) against the reported fatigue/cognition efficacy findings to weigh retreatment risk-benefit, while the simulator flags that no cost or productivity data exist in this source.

A patient/advocate user could see, side by side but explicitly not pooled, how the four trials differed in enrolled population and follow-up window, to understand why 'the trials found no benefit' is a more limited and contested claim than commonly presented in guidelines.

spec.title: Lyme Disease Retreatment Trials: Adverse Events and Efficacy Signals (2012 Review)
spec.boundary: This simulation reflects only the trial-level enrollment counts and adverse-event figures reported in a 2012 biostatistical review of two of the four NIH-funded Lyme disease retreatment RCTs it covers (Krupp et al. STOP-LD and Fallon et al.). It does not include any dollar costs, productivity loss, diagnostic-delay burden, or population prevalence figures, because the source document reports none of these. The four trials enrolled structurally different populations and used different follow-up windows, so their results are kept separate here and must not be pooled into one figure.

takeaway.patient: In the two placebo-controlled retreatment trials this document reviewed, adverse events were not rare: about 11% of patients in the Krupp fatigue trial and about 19% of patients in the Fallon cognitive trial had a significant adverse event, including serious events like sepsis and anaphylaxis. The Krupp trial found a real, statistically significant fatigue benefit from retreatment, while the Fallon trial's cognitive-function result was only borderline and did not hold up over time - these are two different trials, with different symptoms and outcomes, so evidence of benefit for fatigue does not mean the same evidence exists for cognitive symptoms.
takeaway.care: This review highlights that the adverse-event burden in the two smaller NIH-funded retreatment trials (Krupp n=55, Fallon n=37) was non-trivial and included serious events (sepsis, anaphylaxis) that should be weighed in shared decision-making, alongside genuinely mixed efficacy signals: a statistically significant fatigue benefit in Krupp versus a borderline, non-sustained cognitive-function result in Fallon. The document argues these trials were often underpowered, so a flat 'no benefit' framing drawn from guidelines may understate the real uncertainty in the evidence base.
takeaway.policy: The trial evidence underlying guideline recommendations against Lyme disease retreatment comes from four structurally different, often small and likely underpowered RCTs (Klempner seropositive n=78, seronegative n=51; Krupp n=55; Fallon n=37). This review's own adverse-event figures (6 of 55 significant events, 4 serious, in Krupp; an 18.9% adverse-event rate in Fallon) combined with a statistically significant fatigue benefit in Krupp and a marginal, non-sustained cognitive benefit in Fallon, suggest the evidence base supporting current 'no retreatment benefit' guidance is more contested and less uniform than a single pooled verdict implies.

patient: When discussing retreatment with a clinician, ask what is known about adverse-event risk specifically for the symptom being targeted (fatigue versus cognitive symptoms), since these two trials found different levels of evidence for benefit.
Ask whether any of the serious events reported in these trials (such as sepsis or a severe allergic reaction) are relevant to your own health history before deciding on retreatment.
Raise with your clinician which specific trial and symptom type is being referenced when you're told 'the trials found no benefit,' since that is a more limited and contested claim than it may sound.
care: This finding may be worth checking against how your team currently frames retreatment risk-benefit conversations - specifically whether fatigue and cognitive-symptom evidence are being presented as equivalent when the trials found different results for each.

Consider whether informed-consent materials distinguish adverse-event risk by trial and outcome type (Krupp fatigue trial vs. Fallon cognitive trial) rather than citing a single pooled 'trials show no benefit' statement.
Review whether counseling on IV ceftriaxone retreatment accounts for the serious adverse events reported in these trials (sepsis, anaphylaxis).
policy: Guideline panels could consider commissioning adequately powered replication trials stratified by symptom domain (fatigue vs. cognitive impairment) rather than relying on pooled summaries of these four structurally different trials.

Policy reviewers could flag that no cost, utilization, or productivity-loss data exist in this evidence base, so any economic argument for or against retreatment coverage needs a separate cost-of-illness source.
Consider commissioning an independent statistical power review of the four existing trials before using them as sole justification for coverage or guideline decisions.

inputs.label: Krupp STOP-LD trial: total enrolled patients
inputs.source: Document Section 3.2.1 states 55 patients enrolled (28 ceftriaxone, 27 placebo); the 50-60 range is an assumed exploration bound, not from the source.
inputs.interpretation: This is the total enrollment in the Krupp STOP-LD trial; it is the denominator for the adverse-event rate below, so moving it shows how sensitive a reported trial safety rate is to the small size of this trial.

inputs.label: Krupp trial: significant adverse events (both arms)
inputs.source: Document Section 3.2.1 reports 6 significant adverse events; the 4-8 range is an assumed exploration bound, not from the source.
inputs.interpretation: This is the document's reported count of clinically significant adverse events across both arms of the Krupp trial; it drives the adverse-event rate output and its minimum is set so it can never fall below the serious-event count, preserving the document's reported subset relationship.

inputs.label: Krupp trial: serious adverse events (subset)
inputs.source: Document Section 3.2.1 reports 4 serious events (3 sepsis in placebo arm, 1 anaphylaxis in ceftriaxone arm); the 0-4 range is an assumed exploration bound, not from the source.
inputs.interpretation: This is the subset of the significant adverse events above that the document classifies as serious; its maximum is capped so it can never exceed the significant-event count, since serious events are a subset of that total.

inputs.label: Fallon trial: total enrolled patients
inputs.source: Document Section 3.3.1 states 37 patients enrolled (23 ceftriaxone, 14 placebo); the 32-42 range is an assumed exploration bound, not from the source.
inputs.interpretation: This is the total enrollment in the Fallon trial; it is the denominator for the Fallon adverse-event rate below.

inputs.label: Fallon trial: total adverse events
inputs.source: Document Section 3.3.1 reports 7 adverse events (18.9% of 37 patients); the 6-9 range is an assumed exploration bound, not from the source.
inputs.interpretation: This is the document's reported adverse-event count in the Fallon trial; its minimum is set so it can never fall below the ceftriaxone-arm count, preserving the document's reported subset relationship.

inputs.label: Fallon trial: adverse events in ceftriaxone arm
inputs.source: Document Section 3.3.1 states 6 of the 7 adverse events occurred in the ceftriaxone arm; the 0-6 range is an assumed exploration bound, not from the source.
inputs.interpretation: This is the number of Fallon trial adverse events that occurred specifically in the active-treatment (ceftriaxone) arm rather than placebo; its maximum is capped so it can never exceed the total adverse-event count.

outputs.label: Krupp trial significant adverse-event rate (% of enrolled patients, both arms combined)
outputs.interpretation: This is the share of all 55 enrolled Krupp STOP-LD patients who experienced a significant adverse event (about 10.9% at default values), combining both the ceftriaxone and placebo arms. The document does not separate how many of these events were caused specifically by the study drug versus occurring in the placebo arm, so this rate describes overall trial safety signal, not treatment-attributable risk alone.

outputs.label: Krupp trial: serious adverse events as share of significant adverse events
outputs.interpretation: This is the share of the Krupp trial's significant adverse events that were serious (about 66.7% at default values) - three sepsis cases in the placebo arm and one anaphylaxis case in the ceftriaxone arm. A higher value signals that among the relatively few adverse events this small trial recorded, most were serious; note most of the serious events reported here actually occurred in the placebo group, not the treated group.

outputs.label: Fallon trial adverse-event rate (% of enrolled patients, both arms combined)
outputs.interpretation: This is the document's reported adverse-event rate in the Fallon trial (about 18.9% at default values), the trial whose own cognitive-function result was only at the margin of statistical significance and was not sustained over time. Because the trial's own primary outcome did not show a clearly sustained benefit, this rate represents harm recorded in a trial that did not establish durable benefit for the cognitive impairment it targeted.

outputs.label: Fallon trial: adverse events occurring in the ceftriaxone arm as share of all Fallon adverse events
outputs.interpretation: This is the share of the Fallon trial's adverse events that occurred specifically in the ceftriaxone (active antibiotic) arm rather than placebo (about 85.7% at default values). Combined with the trial's only marginal, non-sustained cognitive benefit, a higher value here illustrates that most of the recorded harm in this trial fell on patients receiving the antibiotic whose benefit for cognitive impairment was not clearly established.

scenarios.label: Fallon: events mostly in placebo arm
scenarios.goal: Tests how concentrated the Fallon trial's adverse-event signal was in the antibiotic-treated arm.
scenarios.description: Sets the ceftriaxone-arm adverse-event count to 1 (the trial's own placebo-arm figure) to show the arm-share result if most events had instead occurred in the placebo arm, the reverse of the reported 6-of-7 split.

scenarios.label: Krupp: no serious events (illustrative)
scenarios.goal: Tests how much of the Krupp trial's safety concern depended specifically on the serious subset (sepsis, anaphylaxis).
scenarios.description: Sets the Krupp serious adverse-event count to an illustrative lower bound of 0, showing the serious-event share if none of the documented events had been classified as serious, not an alternative the trial itself reported.

package.documentation:
## Data Sources and Parameters

All inputs are drawn from a 2012 biostatistical review of four NIH-funded, placebo-controlled randomized trials evaluating antibiotic retreatment for persistent Lyme disease symptoms (two Klempner trials, Krupp et al. STOP-LD, and Fallon et al.). This simulator models only the enrollment and adverse-event counts the document reports for the Krupp and Fallon trials; it contains no dollar costs, productivity-loss, or population prevalence figures because the source document reports none of these.

- Krupp STOP-LD trial: 55 enrolled patients (28 ceftriaxone, 27 placebo), with 6 reported significant adverse events (4 serious: 3 sepsis cases in the placebo arm, 1 anaphylaxis case in the ceftriaxone arm).
- Fallon trial: 37 enrolled patients (23 ceftriaxone, 14 placebo), with 7 reported adverse events (18.9%), 6 of which occurred in the ceftriaxone arm.

The Krupp trial found a statistically significant fatigue benefit from retreatment; the Fallon trial's cognitive-function result was only at the margin of statistical significance and was not sustained at later follow-up. These two trials measured different symptom domains, used different entry criteria, and followed patients over different time windows, so their adverse-event rates and efficacy findings are modeled separately and must not be pooled into one figure. Input ranges beyond each observed default are assumed exploration bounds chosen to preserve the document's reported subset relationships (serious events within significant events; ceftriaxone-arm events within total events), not additional data from the source.

## Limitations

**Subgroup disaggregation:** The adverse-event counts for both trials are reported only as single pooled trial-arm figures, with no breakdown by sex, age, race/ethnicity, or disability status. Federal survey data sources such as MEPS, NHIS, or BRFSS generally support disaggregated analysis even though this document did not perform one.

**Systemic evidence gap:** The document notes that no sensitive laboratory test for active Lyme (B. burgdorferi) infection currently exists, so treatment guidelines rely entirely on these four RCTs - which the authors argue were often underpowered or analyzed with statistically inefficient methods - rather than on a validated diagnostic pathway. This is a limitation of the evidence-generating system itself, separate from the accuracy of any single figure modeled here.

## Scope

This document is a methodological critique of trial design and statistical power, not a cost-of-illness or economic-burden study. No claims-based undercounting or research-funding-gap limitation applies, because the document does not address insurance claims data or research funding levels.

spec.title: Lyme Disease Retreatment Trials: Adverse Events and Efficacy Signals (2012 Review)
spec.boundary: This simulation reflects only the trial-level enrollment counts and adverse-event figures reported in a 2012 biostatistical review of two of the four NIH-funded Lyme disease retreatment RCTs it covers (Krupp et al. STOP-LD and Fallon et al.). It does not include any dollar costs, productivity loss, diagnostic-delay burden, or population prevalence figures, because the source document reports none of these. The four trials enrolled structurally different populations and used different follow-up windows, so their results are kept separate here and must not be pooled into one figure.

takeaway.patient: In the two placebo-controlled retreatment trials this document reviewed, adverse events were not rare: about 11% of patients in the Krupp fatigue trial and about 19% of patients in the Fallon cognitive trial had a significant adverse event, including serious events like sepsis and anaphylaxis. The Krupp trial found a real, statistically significant fatigue benefit from retreatment, while the Fallon trial's cognitive-function result was only borderline and did not hold up over time - these are two different trials, with different symptoms and outcomes, so evidence of benefit for fatigue does not mean the same evidence exists for cognitive symptoms.
takeaway.care: This review highlights that the adverse-event burden in the two smaller NIH-funded retreatment trials (Krupp n=55, Fallon n=37) was non-trivial and included serious events (sepsis, anaphylaxis) that should be weighed in shared decision-making, alongside genuinely mixed efficacy signals: a statistically significant fatigue benefit in Krupp versus a borderline, non-sustained cognitive-function result in Fallon. The document argues these trials were often underpowered, so a flat 'no benefit' framing drawn from guidelines may understate the real uncertainty in the evidence base.
takeaway.policy: The trial evidence underlying guideline recommendations against Lyme disease retreatment comes from four structurally different, often small and likely underpowered RCTs (Klempner seropositive n=78, seronegative n=51; Krupp n=55; Fallon n=37). This review's own adverse-event figures (6 of 55 significant events, 4 serious, in Krupp; an 18.9% adverse-event rate in Fallon) combined with a statistically significant fatigue benefit in Krupp and a marginal, non-sustained cognitive benefit in Fallon, suggest the evidence base supporting current 'no retreatment benefit' guidance is more contested and less uniform than a single pooled verdict implies.

patient: When discussing retreatment with a clinician, ask what is known about adverse-event risk specifically for the symptom being targeted (fatigue versus cognitive symptoms), since these two trials found different levels of evidence for benefit.
Ask whether any of the serious events reported in these trials (such as sepsis or a severe allergic reaction) are relevant to your own health history before deciding on retreatment.
Raise with your clinician which specific trial and symptom type is being referenced when you're told 'the trials found no benefit,' since that is a more limited and contested claim than it may sound.
care: This finding may be worth checking against how your team currently frames retreatment risk-benefit conversations - specifically whether fatigue and cognitive-symptom evidence are being presented as equivalent when the trials found different results for each.

Consider whether informed-consent materials distinguish adverse-event risk by trial and outcome type (Krupp fatigue trial vs. Fallon cognitive trial) rather than citing a single pooled 'trials show no benefit' statement.
Review whether counseling on IV ceftriaxone retreatment accounts for the serious adverse events reported in these trials (sepsis, anaphylaxis).
policy: Guideline panels could consider commissioning adequately powered replication trials stratified by symptom domain (fatigue vs. cognitive impairment) rather than relying on pooled summaries of these four structurally different trials.

Policy reviewers could flag that no cost, utilization, or productivity-loss data exist in this evidence base, so any economic argument for or against retreatment coverage needs a separate cost-of-illness source.
Consider commissioning an independent statistical power review of the four existing trials before using them as sole justification for coverage or guideline decisions.

inputs.label: Krupp STOP-LD trial: total enrolled patients
inputs.source: Document Section 3.2.1 states 55 patients enrolled (28 ceftriaxone, 27 placebo); the 50-60 range is an assumed exploration bound, not from the source.
inputs.interpretation: This is the total enrollment in the Krupp STOP-LD trial; it is the denominator for the adverse-event rate below, so moving it shows how sensitive a reported trial safety rate is to the small size of this trial.

inputs.label: Krupp trial: significant adverse events (both arms)
inputs.source: Document Section 3.2.1 reports 6 significant adverse events; the 4-8 range is an assumed exploration bound, not from the source.
inputs.interpretation: This is the document's reported count of clinically significant adverse events across both arms of the Krupp trial; it drives the adverse-event rate output and its minimum is set so it can never fall below the serious-event count, preserving the document's reported subset relationship.

inputs.label: Krupp trial: serious adverse events (subset)
inputs.source: Document Section 3.2.1 reports 4 serious events (3 sepsis in placebo arm, 1 anaphylaxis in ceftriaxone arm); the 0-4 range is an assumed exploration bound, not from the source.
inputs.interpretation: This is the subset of the significant adverse events above that the document classifies as serious; its maximum is capped so it can never exceed the significant-event count, since serious events are a subset of that total.

inputs.label: Fallon trial: total enrolled patients
inputs.source: Document Section 3.3.1 states 37 patients enrolled (23 ceftriaxone, 14 placebo); the 32-42 range is an assumed exploration bound, not from the source.
inputs.interpretation: This is the total enrollment in the Fallon trial; it is the denominator for the Fallon adverse-event rate below.

inputs.label: Fallon trial: total adverse events
inputs.source: Document Section 3.3.1 reports 7 adverse events (18.9% of 37 patients); the 6-9 range is an assumed exploration bound, not from the source.
inputs.interpretation: This is the document's reported adverse-event count in the Fallon trial; its minimum is set so it can never fall below the ceftriaxone-arm count, preserving the document's reported subset relationship.

inputs.label: Fallon trial: adverse events in ceftriaxone arm
inputs.source: Document Section 3.3.1 states 6 of the 7 adverse events occurred in the ceftriaxone arm; the 0-6 range is an assumed exploration bound, not from the source.
inputs.interpretation: This is the number of Fallon trial adverse events that occurred specifically in the active-treatment (ceftriaxone) arm rather than placebo; its maximum is capped so it can never exceed the total adverse-event count.

outputs.label: Krupp trial significant adverse-event rate (% of enrolled patients, both arms combined)
outputs.interpretation: This is the share of all 55 enrolled Krupp STOP-LD patients who experienced a significant adverse event (about 10.9% at default values), combining both the ceftriaxone and placebo arms. The document does not separate how many of these events were caused specifically by the study drug versus occurring in the placebo arm, so this rate describes overall trial safety signal, not treatment-attributable risk alone.

outputs.label: Krupp trial: serious adverse events as share of significant adverse events
outputs.interpretation: This is the share of the Krupp trial's significant adverse events that were serious (about 66.7% at default values) - three sepsis cases in the placebo arm and one anaphylaxis case in the ceftriaxone arm. A higher value signals that among the relatively few adverse events this small trial recorded, most were serious; note most of the serious events reported here actually occurred in the placebo group, not the treated group.

outputs.label: Fallon trial adverse-event rate (% of enrolled patients, both arms combined)
outputs.interpretation: This is the document's reported adverse-event rate in the Fallon trial (about 18.9% at default values), the trial whose own cognitive-function result was only at the margin of statistical significance and was not sustained over time. Because the trial's own primary outcome did not show a clearly sustained benefit, this rate represents harm recorded in a trial that did not establish durable benefit for the cognitive impairment it targeted.

outputs.label: Fallon trial: adverse events occurring in the ceftriaxone arm as share of all Fallon adverse events
outputs.interpretation: This is the share of the Fallon trial's adverse events that occurred specifically in the ceftriaxone (active antibiotic) arm rather than placebo (about 85.7% at default values). Combined with the trial's only marginal, non-sustained cognitive benefit, a higher value here illustrates that most of the recorded harm in this trial fell on patients receiving the antibiotic whose benefit for cognitive impairment was not clearly established.

scenarios.label: Fallon: events mostly in placebo arm
scenarios.goal: Tests how concentrated the Fallon trial's adverse-event signal was in the antibiotic-treated arm.
scenarios.description: Sets the ceftriaxone-arm adverse-event count to 1 (the trial's own placebo-arm figure) to show the arm-share result if most events had instead occurred in the placebo arm, the reverse of the reported 6-of-7 split.

scenarios.label: Krupp: no serious events (illustrative)
scenarios.goal: Tests how much of the Krupp trial's safety concern depended specifically on the serious subset (sepsis, anaphylaxis).
scenarios.description: Sets the Krupp serious adverse-event count to an illustrative lower bound of 0, showing the serious-event share if none of the documented events had been classified as serious, not an alternative the trial itself reported.
